species.description:
Standing order, Security Chief D. Okafor.

Do not engage critters. They spook easily and most will move off if you give them room. The ones that don't are the problem. They bite first, then swing the tail. The tail club is what killed Haskins in Gallery 4, and his suit made no difference.

They stand three to four meters, blue bark, six eyes, two legs. Three kinds. Drudges are the smaller ones, mostly bare bark with one patch of shell. Sires are fully plated. The matriarch is the big one, wider than a hatch door, and she is the only one that lays. If you find eggs, she is close. Back out the way you came and call it in. Leave the eggs alone.

They weigh less than you'd think for the height, 90 to 130 kilos. Nothing else down here has killed as many of us.
species.notes:
Standing order, Security Chief D. Okafor.

Do not engage critters. Most of the time they back off when the lamps come up. The ones that don't are the problem. They bite first, then swing the tail. The tail club is what killed Haskins in Gallery 4, and his suit made no difference.

Three kinds. Drudges are smaller, mostly bare bark with one patch of shell, and they're the ones you'll see foraging. Sires are fully plated and taller. The matriarch is the big one, wider than a hatch door, and she is the only one that lays. If you find eggs, she is close. Back out the way you came and call it in. Leave the eggs alone.

They weigh less than you'd think for the height, 90 to 130 kilos, so they are quick. Six eyes. Possibly weak in bright light. Not confirmed.

species.description:
Writing this down because nobody believes me about the size.

Knee height. Maybe hip height on a big one. People hear "small" and relax, and that's how Petra got hurt. It came out of the dark on three legs, this low crawling lurch, and the armor caught my headlamp. Purple, then green, then purple again. Pretty, honestly, right up until it opened its arms.

Four arms, all claws. It went for her legs first, then put its head down and used the horns. Three horns. Six eyes. I counted afterwards, on the one Ruiz shot.

It has wings. I've never seen one fly. They stay folded flat against its back the whole time. Maybe they can't. I don't want to find out.

They hunt us. They don't stumble into you, they come looking. If you see that color on the rock, it's not ore.

species.description:
Phoboraptor velox. Dr. M. Lindqvist, xenobiology.

The grelk is a monopod. It moves by hopping and covers ground much faster than the gait suggests; one crossed Chamber 9 in under four seconds. Standing height runs 2.5 to 4 m, mass 71 to 113 kg, so the animal is tall and comparatively light.

The pelt is long, coarse and rust red, close enough to the cavern walls that a resting grelk is easy to walk past. Among the hair are a few stiff quills. There is a single forelimb, offset to one side. Six eyes, in two rows. Adults carry branching antlers of ten tines.

Young are born live. Joeys are about a fifth of adult size, already on their one leg, with small antlers of five tines and a few quills of their own.

Grelks hunt people. They gore with the antlers and bite. Please do not approach a resting adult for a tissue sample. I have now asked twice.

species.description:
From the hydroponics crew, for whoever has night rotation.

The blobs are scared of you. That sounds like good news until you remember it's three meters tall and weighs as much as two of us, and scared things don't look where they're going. Six eyes, every one of them on you, and it still backs straight into the irrigation lines.

The skin is slimy and shines every color at once. Whatever it brushes past ends up slick. Wipe the handles before you grab anything.

Two arms with blunt nubs on the ends, nothing sharp. Four legs. The bite is what you need to watch. Get too close, or box one in, and it will bite.

So: leave it a way out, give it room, and wait. It'll go.
species.notes:
From the hydroponics crew, for whoever has night rotation.

The blobs are scared of you. That sounds like good news until you remember it's three meters tall and weighs as much as two of us, and scared things don't look where they're going. Six eyes, every one of them on you, and it still backs straight into the irrigation lines.

The skin is slick and shines every color at once. It leaves a film on anything it touches. The film does not come off tool handles, so don't bother.

Two arms with blunt nubs on the ends, nothing sharp. Four short legs. The bite is what you need to watch. Corner one and it will bite, and it doesn't let go fast.

So: leave it a way out, turn your lamp down, and wait. It'll go.

species.description:
Deep Survey orientation. Read before your first descent.

Count the arms. That's how you tell a stingtail's age, and the age tells you how bad your day is about to get.

Grub: one arm, one leg, two little horns. About a tenth the size of an adult. Mostly a nuisance.
Nymph: two arms, still on one leg, five horns, a tail, and a stinger. Half adult size. Keep your gloves on.
Instar: three arms, now on two legs, seven horns, and the tail ends in a stinger. Nearly full size. Back away.
Adult: four arms, a crown of ten horns, and a barbed stinger. Leave the area.

None of them come up past your waist. Doesn't matter. Adults hunt people. They bite, they gore and they sting, usually all three. Four eyes, if you get close enough to count, which you shouldn't.

The green chitin shows up well against the rock, so most of the time you'll see one before it sees you. Use that.

species.description:
Survey log, lower galleries. You will usually see a tinehorn's eyes before anything else: three of them, two set wide and one high on the brow, catching your lamp from the dark of the cavern roof. The rest of it is easy to lose. Its skin is a smooth, unbroken black, and it has no legs at all; it hangs in the air on a pair of wings, its long body trailing beneath it into a tail that ends in a stinger.

They are not large. A grown one stands somewhere between 0.6 and 1.4 m (2'0"-4'6") and weighs 21-48 kg (46-106 lb), and nearly all of that is nerve. Tinehorns are skittish around people and will usually keep their distance. Do not mistake that for harmlessness. Crowd one and it turns everything it has on you at once: a bite, six arms that wrap and strangle, a crown of branching antlers with ten tines driven forward like a rack of spikes, and that stinger curling up over its back.

Standing advice for work crews: if a tinehorn is watching you, give it room and let it leave first. Adults are recognizable at a glance by the antlers. Count the arms if you have to: six. If you're close enough to count, you're too close.
species.notes:
Tinehorn (Leiophis volans), seed 1293250282, single adult form.

Accepted sprite: db3rjo0a5kmtg161d8kg (2026-10-08). Revision of db3rdv8a5kmtg161d8k0 with the smile line removed, fangs kept.
- Read as a legless, serpentine flier: reared-up trunk coiling at the base, hovering on spread bat wings. Name ("smooth snake, flying") drove the body plan.
- Countable check: 3 eyes (two wide + one on brow), 6 arms (3 per side), 0 legs, 2 wings, 1 tail with red stinger, antlers 5 tines per side = 10.
- Cautious temperament: arms raised defensively, eyes wide with small pupils. Attacks visible: fangs (bite), arms (strangle), antlers (gore), stinger (sting).
- Legibility: black body (#1b1922) gets a cool grey rim (#6e6884) so it holds up on fog (#2e0d0b); antlers are bone-colored with a dark outline for the orange floor.
- Palette: black, grey rim, wing violet, antler bone, eye yellow, stinger red (6).

Description rewritten as a survey-log entry; all facts kept to the generated traits.

species.description:
Posted at every airlock below Level 3, by order of colony security:

THE ET HUNTS PEOPLE.

It is not shy, and it is not curious. If it has seen you, it is coming for you.

KNOW IT ON SIGHT. White fur, bright against the red rock, so you will see it before it reaches you. Use that time. Six eyes. Four arms. No legs: it slithers, and it is faster than it looks. A grown ET stands 2.2-4.5 m (7'4"-14'9") and weighs 152-306 kg (335-675 lb). You cannot hold a door against it alone.

KNOW HOW IT KILLS. Adults carry hooked claws and rake with them. They seize with all four arms and strangle. The tail ends in a stinger, and it will use it while its arms hold you.

DO NOT go out alone. DO NOT go after one that has gone back into the dark. Report every sighting, however far off.
species.notes:
ET (Leucotherium album), seed 153978240, single adult form. Picked from a 4-roll preview as a hostile counterpoint to the tinehorn: big, white, legless, a hunter.

Accepted sprite: db3vbgoa5kmtg161d8n0 (2026-10-08). Fourth pass per Kevin: earlier versions read too ghost-like, so the lower body is a long furred tube coiled underneath instead of a tapering blob; tail points down.
- Torso narrows into a coil wrapped under the body; the tail leaves the coil on the right and tapers as it hangs downward.
- Arms poised to strike: elbows out, forearms raised, a parallel pair of hooked claws per hand curving inward.
- Stinger is a hook drawn exactly like the claws (dark outline, lilac core), pointing down at the tail tip.
- Countable check: 6 eyes (two rows of 3), 4 arms (2 per side), 0 legs, 0 wings, 1 tail ending in a stinger.
- Hostile temperament: angry V brow, open fanged maw, cocked arms.
- Fur: zigzag rows across the chest, short brush ticks along the coil.
- Legibility: white fur (#f2efe9) with a heavy dark outline (#241a24) for the orange floor; reads by value on fog.
- Palette: white, lilac (#c9c3d6, claws, stinger, fur marks), outline, red eyes (#e8352b).

Description rewritten as a colony-security warning notice; facts kept to the generated traits.

species.description:
Field note: stingtails (orange stone). Not the small green ones.

This is the big stingtail: craggy orange stone, 2.6-3.4 m (8'8"-11'1") tall and 142-183 kg (313-403 lb). Four eyes, no legs at all, and eight arms. A patch of shell sits on the body, and the tail ends in a stinger.

Stingtails are skittish and would rather not fight. If you leave them no choice, they will bite, strangle you with those eight arms, and sting. Do not be the one who finds out what that looks like.

Two stages: an egg, and then the adult. Adults lay the eggs.

species.description:
Welcome-wagon notice: greens.

Good news, for once. Greens interact well with humans, and you can walk up to one without the usual paperwork. They stand 1.8-3.8 m (6'0"-12'6") and weigh 55-115 kg (121-254 lb), covered head to foot in green armor plates. Two eyes, three arms, and a single leg, which they manage perfectly well.

Greens are the friendly ones. Say hello. Mind the size, though: the big ones are tall enough to look down on a first-floor window.

Single form.

species.description:
Geology note, Sector 7 west face. Add "rocklings" to the hazard list.

They look quarried, not grown: craggy red stone, 2.3-3.2 m (7'5"-10'6") tall, 149-211 kg (328-465 lb). Four eyes, two arms, three legs. Branching antlers of seven tines crown the head.

Rocklings are skittish around people and will usually keep their distance. Do not test that. Pushed, a rockling bites, wraps its arms around you to strangle, and gores with the antlers. It has the weight to make all three count.

Single form, no young seen. Do not chip a sample off the antlers, whatever the lab asks.

species.description:
WARNING NOTICE: SHIMMER. Do not admire it.

The skin is slimy and iridescent, and it does throw off a lovely colour against the cavern rock. That is the last nice thing in this notice. A shimmer stands 1.1-2.4 m (3'6"-7'11") and weighs 35-81 kg (77-179 lb). It has two eyes, three arms, and five legs, and it hunts people.

It will bite you. It will gore you with the single nub of a horn on its head. It will sting you with a barbed stinger. Overlapping shell plates and a ridge of spines mean there is not much of it you can safely grab either.

Single form, no tail, no wings. If you can see the colours, you are too close.

species.description:
Maintenance log, Tunnel 12. Gremlins, for those of you new to the crew.

Gremlins run 1.5-2.2 m (4'10"-7'2") and 99-146 kg (218-322 lb), which is a lot of animal. Purple chitin, three eyes, five legs, a tail, and exactly one arm. They are skittish and mostly avoid people. Box one in and it will rake you with its claw and sting you with its tail.

The nymph is about a third of adult size, on three legs with a tail and a patch of shell. It has no arm yet; that comes later.

Adults come in three castes, all with a stinger on the tail. Drudges are the smallest and keep just a patch of shell. Sires carry a full carapace. Matriarchs, the largest, carry a full carapace as well, and only matriarchs bear young.

If the lights flicker, check the lights first.

species.description:
HAZARD BULLETIN: QUILLBACK. Single form. There is no juvenile to confuse it with.

The quillback is small, 0.5-1.5 m (1'8"-4'11") and 14-42 kg (31-93 lb), and that is the most dangerous thing about it, because people do not take it seriously. It crawls on three legs with its wings folded, and it has four eyes, two powerful arms, and a tail. The slimy pale skin stands out against the Martian rock, so you will see it coming. It will not matter.

A crown of eight horns on the head, a coat of quills down the back. Quillbacks hunt people. They bite, and they gore with the horns.

If you see one, do not try to measure it.

Melanocarcinus multipes, "squid" to everyone below Level 6, though nothing about it is soft.

An adult stands 2.3-3.9 m (7'5"-12'9") and weighs 84-144 kg (185-317 lb). Black chitin, three eyes, two arms, six legs, and a tail. Squids are skittish and would rather not meet you. Corner one and it will try everything it has: it bites, rakes with its claws, thrashes its tail, and strangles with its arms.

Three stages. The egg comes first. The nymph is nearly adult size already, with five legs, one arm, a tail, and a patch of shell; the second arm and the sixth leg arrive with maturity.

Adults split into three castes. Drudges are the smallest and keep the patch of shell. Sires are larger, with overlapping shell plates. Matriarchs are the largest of all, also plated, and only matriarchs lay eggs.

species.description:
Jigglers: a word from the mess hall, before someone gets hurt.

No, it's not dessert. A jiggler stands 1.5-3.1 m (4'10"-10'3") and weighs 86-183 kg (190-403 lb), and it is made of quivering green jelly with one large eye, four arms, three legs, and a pair of wings. It is not a snack and it is not a toy.

Jigglers are skittish around people. Give one room and it will usually take the hint. Crowd it and it lashes out, raking with its claws, and with four arms that is a great deal of raking.

Their life is short on steps: an egg, then the adult. Adults lay the eggs. If you find one, leave it where it is and report it.

species.description:
Deep Survey field log, Aviary Cavern.

The harpy is smaller than the name suggests: 0.6-0.9 m (2'0"-2'11") and 33-48 kg (73-106 lb). It crawls on four legs with its wings folded tight, and it has six eyes, which is five more than you want looking at you. The yellow feathers disappear against the rock.

Harpies hunt people. They bite, and they gore with their horns.

Learn the castes before you learn anything else.
Hatchling: about a fifth of adult size, on two legs, with three horns, a few quills, and a patch of shell. No wings yet.
Drudge: four horns, a ridge of spines, overlapping shell plates.
Sire: five horns, the same spines and plates. Slightly bigger.
Matriarch: by far the largest. A crown of nine horns, a full coat of quills, and a full carapace.

Only matriarchs bear young, so where there is a matriarch there is a nest. Do not get close enough to count the horns.

species.description:
SURVEY LOG — CAVE SYSTEM 7, ENTRY 14

Designation: Birdie (Areornis concolor). Hostile.

Do not let the name fool you. Nothing about this animal is cute. It is a solid green mass of feathers, 2.5 to 3.7 m tall and between 133 and 203 kg, and it moves by hopping on a single leg. It has no wings and does not fly. It has two eyes and exactly one arm, and that arm ends in claws it uses to rake anything it can reach.

Our field team lost a drone and nearly lost a surveyor to one before we understood the pattern: the hopping is quick, the reach of that single arm is long, and it hunts humans actively. Against the red rock the green plumage is conspicuous, which is the only mercy we get. If you see green, turn around.

Adults only; we have found no young. Sprite and further notes pending.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — POSTED AT THE CAVE MOUTH

If you remember one name from the deep caves, make it Bogeyman. Deinomedusa martis. Apex predator. Hostile on sight.

A grown Bogeyman stands 2.3 to 2.7 m and weighs 115 to 134 kg. It is quivering purple jelly with two eyes and three arms, and it hops on a single leg with its wings folded tight. It bites, rakes with its claws, and strangles with those arms. You do not get to pick which.

Young are called spawn: about a fifth of adult height, one leg, one arm, and blunt nubs where the claws will be. They are not safe either, but they are the least of your worries. Adults come in castes. The matriarch is the largest and carries scythe-like claws, and she is the only one who bears young. Drudges and sires are smaller, with hooked claws. All adults hop, all adults have wings, and all of them are lethal.

Nothing else in the caves is as deadly. Every colony child knows the name, and the adults who have met one talk about it quietly, if they talk at all.

species.description:
FIELD NOTES — CHOOK (Megamorphus vorax)

Tall, light, and mean. A Chook stands 2.9 to 3.7 m but weighs only 67 to 86 kg, so it is mostly legs, feathers and bad attitude. The plumage is blue. It has four eyes, which is unsettling in a bird-shaped thing, and three long arms. It strides on two legs rather than hopping or crawling.

It hunts humans. Claws do the raking; the three arms do the strangling. In close quarters those arms are the real danger, since a victim can be clawed and held at the same time.

Life cycle is simple: an egg, then an adult. The egg is inert and no threat on its own. Adults lay eggs, so if you find a clutch, assume a Chook is within sight.

Recommended response: keep distance, keep moving, do not corner one.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — KOBOLD (Nanochelys cavernicola)

A small, nervous cave creature, 0.3 to 0.9 m tall and 13 to 40 kg. Its body is covered in blue armor plates, the color miners once blamed on kobolds and called cobalt. It has six eyes spread across the head, three legs, and a pair of wings. It has no arms. Its hooked claws are used on the ground, not for grabbing.

Kobolds are skittish and want to be left alone. Approach slowly and they will generally retreat. Press them, corner them, or get too close, and they will lash out by biting. The bite is the only attack we have recorded from this species.

Six eyes make it very hard to sneak up on one. If you do want a closer look, announce yourself and keep a clear path behind you.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — MANTICORE (Ceratocheirus elysii)

Hostile, and armed at both ends. Adults run 0.7 to 1.6 m and 36 to 89 kg, covered in a shaggy orange mane that blends well enough into the rock that you will see the horns first. They have five eyes, two arms, and five legs, and they crawl. A tail ending in a stinger trails behind them, which is where the name comes from.

They attack three ways: raking with claws, goring with the crown of 11 horns on the adult's head, and stinging with the tail. Expect to be hit from more than one direction.

Life stages:
- Egg: inert.
- Cub: already about two thirds adult size, with four legs, one arm, a tail with its stinger, and a cluster of 7 horns. Do not mistake it for harmless.
- Adult: the full crown of horns, five legs, two arms. Adults lay eggs.

Stay out of reach of the tail, and do not turn your back.

species.description:
INCIDENT REPORT — WRAITH (Deinocheirus phobos)

Crew name, and it stuck. Pale, feathered, legless, and 1.8 to 3 m long when it rises up, with five eyes and eight arms. It slithers along the ground and weighs 94 to 156 kg.

It is hostile and it hunts humans. All eight arms end in claws, and it kills by raking. There is no wing, no tail and no special trick that we know of; the danger is simply how many arms are reaching for you at once.

Because it has no legs, people tend to assume it is slow. Treat that assumption as unverified until you have measured it from a safe distance.

Only adults have been observed. The pale feathers do show up against the rock, so you may get a moment's warning.

species.description:
FIELD RESEARCHER'S LOG — HART (Cryptoceras fugax)

Cautious rather than hostile. A Hart is big, 2.1 to 2.7 m and 132 to 174 kg, with bony blue skin, three eyes, three arms, and a single leg. It does not hunt people, but it is skittish and it will defend itself if you crowd it: biting, raking with claws, and goring with its two horns and small antlers of four tines.

Like the white hart of the old hunts, it is seen more often than it is caught.

The species hatches from eggs. The eft, which is the juvenile, is already about two thirds adult size, with one leg, two arms, a single nub of a horn, and antlers of just two tines. It is a good illustration of how the adult's headgear develops.

Adults lay eggs. Suggested approach: observe from a distance, make noise before coming into view, and leave if it starts to turn toward you.

species.description:
COLONY SURVEY — BLUECAP (Cyanomorphus utopiae)

A caste species, named for the blue lights miners once followed to good seams. Eggs hatch into squabs, which are nearly adult size (about 70 percent), with four legs, two arms, a tail, a cluster of 7 horns and hooked claws. They then mature into one of three adult castes, all with three arms, five legs, a tail and blue feathers:

- Matriarch: the largest, about one and a half times typical adult size, with a crown of 12 horns and scythe-like claws. She alone lays eggs.
- Sire: slightly larger than a drudge, also with a crown of 12 horns and scythe-like claws.
- Drudge: the smallest, with a crown of 9 horns and hooked claws.

Overall they stand 1 to 2.1 m and weigh 26 to 54 kg. They have three eyes. Temperament is cautious: they are skittish, but when pushed they will bite, rake, strangle and gore.

Do not approach a nest.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — BANSHEE (Pteronycteris cavernicola)

A tall, pale, one-eyed thing with smooth white skin, two arms, three legs, and a pair of wings. Adults stand 2.1 to 2.9 m and weigh 95 to 133 kg. A patch of shell on the body gives it a little armor.

It is cautious by nature. We have not seen it go looking for people. If it feels cornered it will rake with its claws, and with that height and reach you should not test it. The crew named it for the pale woman of the old stories, who is seen before trouble rather than causing it.

The single large eye is the first thing most people notice, and it seems to track movement well, so assume it has seen you before you have seen it. Keep a steady pace, do not rush it, and give it room to leave.

Only adults have been recorded.

species.description:
DANGER ASSESSMENT — GRELK (Iridolestes deimos)

Hostile. A Grelk is 2.5 to 3.6 m of heavy, bony, iridescent skin, weighing 152 to 213 kg. It has five eyes and seven arms, and no legs at all; it slithers. The sheen of its skin catches lamplight and makes it easy to spot, which is some help.

Its attack is the bite. The seven arms are thought to do the holding while the jaws do the damage, but we have not yet seen enough to say exactly how. Treat the whole body as a hazard.

Adult specimens only. Our team recommends keeping to open ground, where a legless creature of this weight has the least advantage, and staying well away from tight passages.

species.description:
WARNING — THE GARGOYLE (Acanthohystrix troglodytes)

You may walk past one. They are 2.4 to 2.6 m tall, weigh 59 to 64 kg, and their craggy orange stone skin and coat of quills blend into the Martian rock. They sit as still as carved stone. Look for five eyes, and for three arms that are too long and too patient.

They crawl on five legs, and they hunt humans. They kill by strangling with the arms. There is no biting, no clawing, no tail; it is all about being held.

Life cycle: egg, then adult. Adults lay eggs, so a chamber with one Gargoyle may be a nursery.

Stay in the lit parts of the cave. Check rock formations before leaning on them.

species.description:
FIELD NOTES — GRINDYLOW (Onychotherium phobos)

Small, green, smooth-skinned, and hostile. An adult Grindylow is 0.6 to 1.2 m tall and 13 to 26 kg, crawling on four legs with two arms. It has five eyes. The arms carry scythe-like claws, but the species kills by biting.

The young are called polliwogs. They are about a fifth of adult size, with two legs, one arm, and only blunt claw nubs where the scythes will grow. Adults bear young rather than laying eggs.

Named for the green thing in the old stories that pulls children into ponds. Do not let the size fool you. A Grindylow will hunt a human, and a group of them in a narrow passage is worse than a single large animal. Keep your legs protected and your back to a wall.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S SKETCH — WISP (Onychomorphus fallax)

A small, winged, quivering blue blob, 0.4 to 0.9 m tall and 19 to 39 kg. It has four eyes, one arm, and four legs, plus a pair of wings. A few quills and scythe-like claws are the only hard parts on it.

Cautious. Wisps keep their distance and will leave if you let them. If you get too close, they lash out by biting; we have not recorded them using the claws or the arm in an attack.

The species name "fallax" means deceptive, and the crew name is in the same spirit: a blue glimmer that draws you off the path. It looks soft and harmless and it is not entirely either. Keep a respectful distance, avoid sudden moves, and do not try to pick one up.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — LINDWORM (Onychodon cavernicola)

Not to be confused with the small blue kobold. This one is yellow-scaled, 1.6 to 2.6 m, 41 to 66 kg, and hostile. It has no legs and slithers like the serpent-dragon it is named for, with three arms tipped with scythe-like claws and six eyes. A pair of wings is kept folded against the body.

It kills by biting and by strangling with its arms.

Young are called elvers: about a tenth of adult size, with one leg, one arm, and blunt claw nubs. Adults bear young. If you see an elver, an adult is likely close.

Move quietly. The yellow scales blend into the rock under poor light.

species.description:
ENTRY — STUMP (Cryptozoon elysii)

At first glance it is a dead tree. White bark, woody body, a single leg like a trunk, and it stands 2.2 to 4 m tall, weighing 142 to 255 kg. Look closer and you find five eyes, four arms, a tail, a pair of wings, and a pair of small antlers with two tines.

Stumps are cautious and skittish. They will not chase you, but they defend themselves by strangling with their arms and goring with their antlers. Only these two attacks have been recorded.

The camouflage is the main hazard. Do not lean on, climb, or tie equipment to unfamiliar trees in the caves. If one blinks, back away.

species.description:
COLONY SURVEY — ERLKING (Leucozoon elysii)

Hostile. White bark, five eyes, no arms, and two legs on which it strides. Adults are 2.2 to 3.2 m tall and 54 to 79 kg. It attacks by biting, and that is all it does.

The life cycle is unusual: a bud about a fifth of adult size with one leg, then an egg, then the adult. Adults come in three castes:

- Matriarch: by far the largest, more than twice a drudge's size. Only she bears young.
- Sire: mid-sized, a little larger than a drudge.
- Drudge: the smallest.

The bark skin makes them stand out pale against the rock, so you should see them before they see you, but do not count on it. They hunt humans. The name comes from the pale king of the alder wood who carries travellers off; keep that in mind and avoid known nesting areas.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — DRYAD (Porphyropteryx fugax)

Variable in size, from 0.9 to 2.2 m and 58 to 153 kg, which means you may meet a small one or a very large one. Purple, woody bark, a single eye, two arms, two legs, and a pair of wings.

It is cautious and skittish; "fugax" means fleeting, and that matches what we see, as they tend to slip away like the tree spirits they were named for. Cornered, they rake with claws and strangle with their arms.

Only adults have been observed. If one retreats, let it. Chasing it into a dead end is how people get hurt.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — BASILISK (Areoceras latens)

Slimy, gray, and tall, 2.4 to 4 m, but light for its size at 48 to 80 kg. It has three eyes and five legs and no arms. The adult wears a crown of 11 horns, which is how it earned the name of the little king of serpents.

Cautious and skittish. If you crowd one, it bites and gores with the crown.

Three life stages, each with more horns and legs:
- Elver: about a fifth of adult size, two legs, three horns.
- Eft: nearly adult size, four legs, a cluster of 7 horns.
- Adult: five legs, the full crown of 11 horns.

Adults bear young. The efts are easy to mistake for adults at a distance, but the horns give them away. Give all stages room.

species.description:
FIELD NOTES — PINCUSHION (Areozoon concolor)

Small and prickly. A Pincushion is 1 to 1.6 m tall and 16 to 25 kg, green-scaled, with a coat of quills. It has four eyes, three arms, and two legs.

Cautious and skittish. It keeps away from people. If you get too close it bites; the quills are not described as an attack, so treat them as defense and handle with care if you must touch one.

Single adult form; no distinct young have been catalogued. A good beginner's creature to observe, as long as you remember it has teeth.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — GREEN MAN (Gigantotitan velox)

Apex predator. Hostile. A Green Man is 3.4 to 3.7 m tall, 137 to 149 kg, covered in green moss, with two eyes, one arm, and one leg on which it hops. It hunts humans, killing by biting and goring with its horns. The matriarch carries three horns; the drudges and sires carry a nub of one.

Life stages: a bud about a third of adult size with one leg; a sporeling, nearly adult size, with two legs and a nub of a horn; then the adults, which come as matriarchs, drudges and sires. Only matriarchs bear young.

The crew named it for the old leaf-faced figure carved over church doors. That one was kinder. The moss blends in poorly against the rock, which is the only advantage we get. Nothing else in the caves is as deadly. Those who have seen one up close do not speak of it lightly.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — SPRIGGAN (Cirrhoraptor longicauda)

Hostile. Small by cave standards, 0.85 to 1.53 m and 41 to 73 kg, but it hops on a single leg and it hunts people. The skin is woody orange bark that blends into the rock. Two eyes, two arms, and a long tail. It rakes with its claws, thrashes the tail, and gores with its horns.

Named for the small woody guardians of the old stories who turn out to be much worse up close.

A caste species with three stages:
- Sporeling: a tenth of adult size, one leg, two horns.
- Squab: nearly adult size, one leg, one arm, a tail, a cluster of 4 horns and blunt claw nubs.
- Adults: matriarch (largest, crown of 9 horns, hooked claws), drudge (smallest, 4 horns, blunt nubs), sire (cluster of 7 horns, hooked claws).

Only matriarchs bear young. If you find a sporeling, an adult is close.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — TARASQUE (Megatitan arcadiae)

A giant, 2.9 to 4.3 m tall, but light for its size at 77 to 114 kg. Gray chitin, six eyes, two arms, four legs, a pair of wings, and a full carapace over the back. It is cautious and skittish and would rather leave than fight; like the shelled dragon of the old Provençal story, it can be calmed by someone patient.

If you corner one, it rakes with its claws and strangles with its arms. Those are the only attacks recorded. The carapace is the main thing to notice when you spot one from a distance: nothing else in the caves has that profile at that height.

Give it room and let it pass. Adults only; no young catalogued.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — THORNHEAD (Leiophis cydoniae)

Smooth red skin, a single eye, four arms, no legs, and a crown of 8 horns. A Thornhead is 0.8 to 1.2 m tall and 38 to 56 kg. It is cautious and skittish, and it does not seek out people.

The trouble is how many ways it can hurt you once it decides to: biting, raking with claws, strangling with its four arms, and goring with the crown. The single eye makes it hard to read where it is looking, so assume it is looking at you.

Single adult form. Keep your distance, keep your hands visible, and do not reach for it.

COLONIST'S WARNING — THE NIGHTMARE (Ostracomonopus utopiae)

Apex predator, though the records call it cautious. 1.4 to 1.7 m of quivering white jelly under a full carapace, 90 to 114 kg, with six eyes, one arm, and one leg. A few quills stand up along the back.

It rakes with its claws, and that is enough. People who have seen what it does with that single arm speak of it quietly; nothing else in the caves is as deadly.

The six eyes cover nearly every angle, so sneaking up on one is not an option, and the white jelly shows pale against the rock. Treat it as a reason to leave an area.

Adults only.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — BARKBACK (Pseudophasma saxicola)

Hostile. A heavy, low crawler of pale-striped bark, 1.8 to 3.5 m and 100 to 195 kg, on six legs, with four eyes and no arms. Overlapping shell plates cover the back.

It has exactly one attack: it bites. Without arms or claws there is nothing else to watch, so the whole danger is in the head and how fast it covers ground. It hunts humans.

The stripes help it vanish against bark-like cave walls, so check formations before stopping to rest. Adults only; nothing else on file.

species.description:
SURVEY LOG — FACHAN (Macromonopus concolor)

Hostile, 2.4 to 2.9 m tall, 122 to 144 kg, and covered in slimy yellow skin that blends into the rock. It has a single eye, a single arm tipped with hooked claws, and a single leg on which it hops, with its wings folded. One of everything, like the Highland monster it is named for.

It rakes with those claws and nothing else, but one arm at that reach is plenty. It hunts humans.

One eye means a narrow field; if you find yourself outside it, move quietly. Adults only recorded.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — PURPLE STINGER (Kentrocyclops arcadiae)

Smooth purple skin, one eye, three arms, no legs, and a barbed stinger. 1.4 to 1.7 m and 36 to 43 kg, so light for what it can do. Cautious and skittish; it does not hunt people.

If pressed, it rakes with its claws, strangles with its arms, and stings. All three are on the table at once, so do not assume a retreat gives you time.

Single adult form. Give it a wide berth and avoid reaching toward it.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S SKETCH — SLUG (Leucomorphus martis)

A slimy white, tailed, seven-legged thing with four eyes and a single arm, 1.1 to 1.4 m tall and 62 to 77 kg. Cautious and skittish. It does not bite or claw; its only attack is thrashing its tail.

Life stages: the young are elvers, about a tenth of adult size, with four legs and a tail but no arms. Adults bear young.

The tail is the thing to stay away from. Approach from the front and keep your distance if you can.

species.description:
FIELD RESEARCHER'S LOG — PIXIE (Ceratobradypus ares)

The friendliest thing we have catalogued so far. A small pale mossy creature, 0.45 to 0.67 m and 30 to 45 kg, with one eye, two arms, one leg, a pair of wings, a cluster of 4 horns, a full carapace and hooked claws. It interacts well with humans and has shown no interest in fighting.

It does have the equipment, though: strangling with its arms and goring with its horns are the recorded attacks, so do not take its manner for granted. Pixies in the old stories were friendly too, until someone was rude.

Life stages: the sporeling is about a third of adult size, with one leg, one arm, 2 horns, a patch of shell and blunt claw nubs. Adults bear young.

Treat it politely.

species.description:
COLONY SURVEY — HYDRA (Ceratochelys amazonis)

Big, 3.2 to 4.2 m and 167 to 218 kg, with iridescent armor plates, one eye, seven arms, a tail and no legs. The seven arms moving at once are where the name comes from. Cautious and skittish. When pushed it strangles with the arms, gores with the horns, and stings.

Stages:
- Larva: about a fifth of adult size, one leg, three arms, a tail, a cluster of 4 horns, a patch of shell, blunt claw nubs and a stinger.
- Matriarch: the largest, a crown of 12 horns, overlapping shell plates, hooked claws and a barbed stinger. Only she bears young.
- Sire: a crown of 10 horns, shell plates, hooked claws, barbed stinger.
- Drudge: the smallest, a cluster of 6 horns, a patch of shell, blunt nubs and a stinger.

All adult castes have seven arms and a tail and slither without legs. Avoid nests.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — SKRELL (Porphyrozoon ares)

Tall for a skittish thing: 1.5 to 2.4 m, 55 to 90 kg. Purple feathers, three eyes, five arms, one leg, a tail and a pair of wings. A few quills and a patch of shell mark the adult. Cautious; it won't start trouble, but if cornered it rakes with its claws and strangles with those five arms.

Nobody is sure who first called it a skrell. It sounds like the noise it makes, though nobody has recorded it making one.

Life stages: the egg is inert, about a quarter of adult size. Adults lay eggs, so a clutch means a parent is near.

Five arms and one leg make the silhouette hard to mistake. Back off slowly.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — IMP (Porphyrodon cavernicola)

Small, and that is the whole trick. An Imp is 0.3 to 0.7 m and 8 to 19 kg of quivering purple jelly, with three eyes, two arms, a tail and no legs, and it is hostile. It slithers up to people and thrashes its tail; that is its only attack.

The jelly glows against the rock, so you will usually see one coming. The trouble is that you may not see the second, third and fourth.

Single adult form.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — FURLONG (Macrotherium multipes)

A furry orange creature of 1.4 to 2.7 m and 65 to 123 kg, on six legs, with two eyes, two arms, a tail and a patch of shell. Cautious and skittish. The crew insists the name is because it is mostly fur and mostly long. Nobody has measured one to check.

Pushed, it rakes with its claws, thrashes its tail, and strangles with its arms: three ways to hurt you, from two directions at once. The fur is thick and dark orange, easy to spot against rock.

Single adult form. Let it leave.

species.description:
FIELD RESEARCHER'S LOG — BROWNIE (Hemeromorphus ares)

One of the friendly ones, and shaggy as the household spirits it is named for. 1.6 to 3 m and 59 to 115 kg, covered in shaggy orange hair, with three eyes, four arms, three legs, a tail and scythe-like claws. It interacts well with humans and has not been recorded going after anyone, though it can thrash the tail and strangle with its arms, so keep a respectful distance.

Life stages: the puggle is about a fifth of adult size, with two legs, two arms, a tail and blunt claw nubs. Adults bear young.

The scythe claws look worse than the temperament.

species.description:
SURVEY LOG — WOLPERTINGER (Poliomorphus elysii)

Smooth gray skin, four eyes, two arms, no legs, and a set of branching antlers with 14 tines. 0.8 to 1.9 m, 55 to 129 kg. Cautious and skittish. Named for the Bavarian joke animal assembled from spare parts, because it looks like one.

Cornered, it rakes with its claws, strangles with its arms, and gores with the antlers. The antlers are the first thing you see and the last thing to get near.

Single adult form.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — URCHIN (Acanthohystrix troglodytes)

A tall, quilled thing: 1.8 to 2.9 m and 73 to 119 kg, with smooth red skin under a coat of quills, four eyes, three arms and five legs. Cautious and skittish, so it keeps away from people. "Urchin" once meant both a hedgehog and a goblin; this is a little of each.

If you get too close it bites and strangles with its arms. The quills are not listed among its attacks, but don't test them.

Single adult form. Walk around it.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — OPAL (Phobolestes ares)

Beautiful and hostile. Smooth iridescent skin, six eyes, six arms and a stride on two legs, 1 to 2.4 m and 63 to 150 kg. It hunts humans, biting and strangling with those six arms.

The iridescence flashes against the rock, which makes it easy to see and very hard to ignore. Six arms means very little room to get free once it has you.

Single adult form.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — CHITTERLING (Phoboraptor unguiculatus)

Hostile. Red chitin that blends into the rock, three eyes, two arms, five legs and a clubbed tail; adults 1.4 to 1.9 m and 81 to 109 kg. It hunts humans: it bites, rakes with its claws, thrashes the club and gores with its horns. The name came from the noise a colony makes. Do not order it at a diner.

Life stages:
- Grub: about a tenth of adult size, three legs, a single nub of a horn.
- Pupa: inert, about half adult size.
- Adults come in castes. The matriarch is the largest (a cluster of 4 horns, scythe-like claws), and only she bears young. The sire is mid-sized (3 horns, hooked claws). The drudge is the smallest (2 horns, blunt claw nubs).

Look for the pupae; the colony is close.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — KELPIE (Areurus olympi)

Blue chitin, three eyes, six arms, a tail, a patch of shell and no legs. 1.8 to 2 m, 79 to 89 kg. Cautious and skittish.

Its one recorded attack is strangling with the arms, and with six of them that is plenty. Like the water spirit it is named for, the danger is in being held and not let go. Leave it room.

Single adult form.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S SKETCH — RED RIPPER (Cryptotherium vigilans)

Small and wary. 0.6 to 1.2 m, 13 to 25 kg, red scales, one eye, three arms with hooked claws, and two legs. Cautious and skittish; if you crowd it, it bites.

Life stages: an inert egg, about a sixth of adult size, then the adult. Adults lay eggs.

Find the eggs and a parent is not far off.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — RED GRIFFIN (Areozoon rubrum)

Hostile. Red feathers that blend into the rock, five eyes, three arms, four legs, a tail and a pair of wings kept folded. 1.6 to 3.6 m, 54 to 123 kg: a wide range, so judge the individual, not the species. It hunts humans and attacks by biting and raking with its claws.

The folded wings should not reassure you; nothing on file says it flies, but nothing says it can't.

Single adult form.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — WIGHT (Areotherium saxicola)

White scales, six eyes, three arms and three legs; 1.7 to 3.5 m, 86 to 174 kg. Cautious and skittish. Its only recorded attack is strangling with the arms.

A big pale shape against dark cave rock, so you should see it first, the way you would a barrow-ghost on a dark hill. Give it the whole corridor.

Single adult form.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S SKETCH — GLOAM (Areotripus martis)

Slimy pale skin, four eyes, three legs and no arms; 0.7 to 1 m, 25 to 36 kg. Cautious and skittish. If you get too close it bites, and that is all it can do.

The name is half from "gloaming" and half from the sound it makes when it moves. It mostly turns up at the edge of the lamplight.

Of everything here, this is the one to simply step around.

Single adult form.

species.description:
COLONY SURVEY — POOKA (Lasiozoon longicauda)

Shaggy purple hair, a single eye, four arms and a tail ending in a stinger; 1 to 1.3 m, 17 to 23 kg. Cautious and skittish, but cornered it does everything: bites, claws, tail, strangling and stinging. Like the shaggy shape-changer it is named for, it is never quite the same animal twice.

Life stages:
- Egg: inert, about a sixth of adult size.
- Cub: about half adult size, one leg, two arms, a tail with the stinger.
- Adults, in castes, have four arms and no legs. The matriarch is the largest and the only one who lays eggs; the sire is mid-sized; the drudge is smallest.

Small, shaggy and well armed. Don't mistake the size for harmlessness.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — SKELLOCK (Phobodon atrox)

Hostile, and not the giant gray tarasque. Shaggy gray-spotted hair, two eyes, two arms and two legs, with overlapping shell plates across the back; 1.1 to 1.6 m, 61 to 90 kg. It hunts humans, and it bites. The name is crew slang; it sounds like shell, skull and hillock at once, and it is a little of each.

The spots break up its outline against the rock. Watch for the shell plates, not the hair.

Single adult form.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — PURPLE GREMLIN (Porphyrozoon concolor)

Woody purple bark, one eye, three arms and three legs; 1.3 to 2.5 m, 56 to 110 kg. Cautious and skittish. If crowded it bites.

Life stages: an inert egg, about a sixth of adult size, then the adult in two forms. The jack is the larger of the pair; the jill is a little smaller and is the one that lays eggs.

Single eye, big body. Step back.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — GRENDEL (Chloropteryx atrox)

Hostile. Slimy green-striped skin, two eyes, eight legs, no arms, a tail and a pair of wings kept folded, with a ridge of spines along the adult; 2.2 to 3 m and 113 to 154 kg. It hunts humans and kills by biting. Named for the old hall-raider, because it comes in from the dark and does not leave quietly.

Life stages:
- Egg: inert, about a fifth of adult size.
- Yearling: roughly half adult size, six legs, a tail, and a few quills.
- Adult: eight legs and the ridge of spines. Adults lay eggs.

Eight legs make it fast over broken ground.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — SHELLBACK (Lasionycteris alata)

Shaggy red hair, four eyes, one arm, one leg and a pair of wings, with a shell on the back; 1.6 to 2.4 m, 74 to 109 kg. Cautious and skittish. If pressed it bites.

Life stages:
- Puggle: about a quarter of adult size, one leg, a patch of shell.
- Joey: most of adult size, two legs, overlapping shell plates.
- Adults, in castes: the matriarch is by far the largest and wears a full carapace; she alone bears young. The sire and drudge are smaller, with overlapping shell plates, and the drudge is the smaller of the two.

Odd-looking and best left alone.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — SNICKERSNEE (Cryptosaurus martis)

Green scales, three eyes, six legs, no arms, and scythe-like claws; 1.2 to 1.9 m, 39 to 59 kg. Cautious and skittish. If crowded it bites.

A snickersnee was an old word for a big knife. The crew borrowed it for the claws, which are not listed among its attacks, but they make the profile unmistakable.

Single adult form.

COLONIST'S WARNING — SKARN (Iridoraptor deimos)

Hostile and enormous: 2.5 to 3 m, but only 62 to 74 kg, craggy iridescent stone with six eyes and six arms and no legs. It hunts humans, biting, raking with its claws and strangling with its arms. The geologists named it after a kind of rock. They will not say which kind or why.

Life stages:
- Egg: inert, about a fifth of adult size.
- Instar: more than half of adult size, four arms, no legs.
- Adult: six arms. Adults lay eggs.

The stone skin flashes in torchlight. If you see it, you are already close.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — DUENDE (Deinomorphus olympi)

Hostile, and tiny: 0.4 to 0.6 m, 12 to 17 kg, bony white skin, three eyes, one arm and three legs, wearing a crown of 11 horns and a patch of shell. It hunts humans, biting and goring with the crown. Named for the little house goblin of Spanish stories, which was never as harmless as its size.

The white bone shows against the rock. Small does not mean safe; it comes at you at knee height.

Single adult form.

species.description:
COLONIST'S WARNING — REDCAP (Pterozoon volans)

Hostile. Quivering red jelly, six eyes, seven arms, one leg, a tail ending in a stinger, a ridge of spines and a pair of wings kept folded; 0.8 to 1.1 m and 51 to 72 kg. It hops on the one leg and hunts humans: raking with claws, thrashing the tail, strangling with the arms, and stinging. The name comes from the murderous little goblin of the border castles, and the resemblance is not just the color.

The red jelly blends into the rock. Four attacks at once, from a creature roughly waist high.

Single adult form.

species.description:
FIELD RESEARCHER'S LOG — MORNINGSTAR (Hemeromorphus utopiae)

Friendly, and big: 1.8 to 2.5 m, 72 to 101 kg, covered in yellow armor plates, with two eyes, four arms, a tail and no legs. The adult carries a spiked tail club. It interacts well with humans; the only attack on record is a bite.

Life stages: the larva is about a quarter of adult size, with two arms and a tail. Adults bear young.

The club looks like a weapon and the temperament says otherwise.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — WHITTLE (Microtetrops troglodytes)

White chitin, four eyes, one arm with scythe-like claws, and four legs; 0.6 to 1.6 m, 14 to 37 kg. Cautious and skittish. If crowded it bites and rakes with its claws.

Small, pale, and carrying one blade, so the crew called it a whittle. It does not carve anything that we know of.

A pale thing in the dark. Leave it room to go.

species.description:
NATURALIST'S ENTRY — BUGBEAR (Cryptotitan fugax)

Large: 2.4 to 3.7 m and 147 to 226 kg, with blue fur, five eyes, three arms, two legs and a stinger. Cautious and skittish. Pressed, it bites and stings. The old bugbear was a hairy thing used to frighten children; this one is mostly frightened of you.

The fur stands out in torchlight. Take that as your warning and go the other way.

Single adult form.

species.description:
HUNTER'S GUIDE — KNUCKER (Deinolestes phobos)

Hostile. Gray bark that blends into the rock, five eyes, three arms and no legs, with a ridge of spines along the back; 1.8 to 2.3 m, 63 to 80 kg. It hunts humans and kills by raking with its claws. Named for the legless water-dragons of the old Sussex stories, said to live in holes too deep to measure.

Life stages: an inert egg, about a fifth of adult size, then the adult. Adults lay eggs.

It slithers, so footsteps won't give it away.

species.description:
FIELD NOTE — WYVERN (Kentrocheirus amazonis)

Bony gray skin, two eyes, two arms, five legs and a pair of wings, with a cluster of 7 horns and a barbed stinger; 1.1 to 2.2 m, 21 to 42 kg. Cautious and skittish. Pressed, it bites, gores and stings. Wings and a barbed sting were enough for the crew to call it a wyvern, even with three legs too many.

Three attacks from one head and one tail end. Keep clear of both.

Single adult form.

species.description:
FIELD RESEARCHER'S LOG — WOODWOSE (Chloromorphus comes)

Friendly. Shaggy green hair, two eyes, six arms, no legs, and small antlers of 5 tines; 1.2 to 1.4 m, 34 to 40 kg. It interacts well with humans. Named for the hairy wild folk of the old forests, who were mostly left alone and mostly left others alone. The recorded attacks are biting, strangling and goring, so keep your distance anyway.

Single adult form.

species.description:
SURVEY LOG — OGRE (Gigantozoon gigas)

Enormous: 3.3 to 4 m and 191 to 235 kg, with bony yellow skin, six eyes, four arms and no legs. Cautious and skittish, which is not what the name suggests. Pressed, it bites, rakes with its claws and strangles with its arms.

Anything this large that is also afraid of you is a problem. Back away without turning.

Single adult form.
